topics.title: Louis Braille: the boy who made dots talk

learn.hook: Can you read a book with your eyes closed? A teenage boy found a way!
points: The lesson 'Braille' tells the story of Louis Braille and his gift to the world.
Louis Braille was born in France in 1809. He lost his sight in an accident when he was a small child.
At his school in Paris, there were very few books that blind students could read.
As a teenager, he made a reading and writing system of raised dots. We call it braille.
World Braille Day is on 4 January, his birthday.

example.q: Read: Louis Braille was born in France in 1809. When he was a small child, an accident hurt his eyes, and he lost his sight. At a school for blind children in Paris, he found very few books he could read. So, when he was only about fifteen, he made a new way of reading with raised dots. Today, people all over the world use braille. Question: Why did Louis Braille make a new way of reading?
steps: Find the line about his school: 'he found very few books he could read.'
He wanted blind people to read easily.
So he made a system of raised dots.
example.answer: Because there were very few books that blind children like him could read.

learn.reallife: Look out for braille dots on lift buttons, some medicine boxes and signs in railway stations and airports.

revise.summary: Louis Braille, born in France in 1809, lost his sight as a small child. As a teenager he made braille, a reading and writing system of raised dots, and World Braille Day is on 4 January.

The problem at his school in Paris

What braille is made of; World Braille Day
traps: He lost his sight, not his voice

learn.hook: Close your eyes and touch a coin. Can you feel its edges? Your fingers can 'see' too!
points: Braille is a code for reading and writing. It is not a separate language.
Each braille letter is made in a cell of 6 dot places: 2 columns of 3.
Different patterns of raised dots stand for different letters, numbers and marks.
The letter 'a' is just one raised dot at the top left of the cell.
Braille is read with the fingertips, moving from left to right. In India, Bharati Braille is used for Indian languages.

example.q: Think it through: a braille cell has 2 columns with 3 dot places in each. How many dot places are there?
steps: Each column has 3 dot places.
There are 2 columns.

learn.reallife: People who are blind also use a white cane to find their way, and talking apps on phones that read text aloud.

revise.summary: Braille is a code for reading and writing, not a separate language. Each letter is a pattern of raised dots in a 6-dot cell, read with the fingertips from left to right.
focus: The braille cell: 2 columns of 3 = 6 dots
remember: Read with fingertips, left to right
'a' = one raised dot at the top left
Bharati Braille is used for Indian languages
traps: Braille is not a language; it is a code
Braille is not read by looking at colours

topics.title: Everyone belongs: inclusion and word beginnings

learn.hook: Ramps, braille signs and kind friends: they help everyone join in!
points: Inclusion means making sure everyone can take part, whatever their abilities.
Ramps, braille signs, talking books and sign language help people join in.
We use kind, respectful words. We say 'a person who is blind' or 'visually impaired'.
A prefix is added at the start of a word to change its meaning: un + kind = unkind.
un-, dis- and im- often mean 'not': unable, unfair, dislike, disagree, impossible, impolite.

example.q: Think it through: Louis Braille showed that reading without sight was not im___. Which word fits?
steps: 'Possible' means it can happen.
The prefix 'im-' means 'not'.
So 'impossible' means it cannot happen. Louis showed it was possible!

learn.reallife: In your class, you can include everyone: pick a new friend for your team, or help a classmate read the board.

quiz.q: What does 'inclusion' mean?
options: Making sure everyone can take part
quiz.explain: Inclusion means no one is left out.
steps: Inclusion = making sure everyone can take part.
Answer: Making sure everyone can take part
quiz.mistake: Confuses inclusion with its opposite

quiz.q: Which of these helps a person in a wheelchair enter a building?
quiz.explain: A ramp is a slope that a wheelchair can roll up.
steps: A wheelchair cannot climb steps.
A ramp is a slope it can roll up.
Answer: A ramp
quiz.mistake: Does not think about the person's needs

quiz.q: What is the opposite of 'kind'?
quiz.explain: un + kind = unkind, which means not kind.
steps: The prefix un- means 'not'.
un + kind = unkind.
Answer: unkind
quiz.mistake: Uses the wrong prefix

quiz.q: Which word means 'not possible'?
quiz.explain: We add 'im-' to 'possible' to make 'impossible'.
steps: im- means 'not'.
im + possible = impossible.
Answer: impossible
quiz.mistake: Uses 'un-' with every word

quiz.q: Which word means 'not agree'?
quiz.explain: dis + agree = disagree.
steps: dis- means 'not'.
dis + agree = disagree.
Answer: disagree
quiz.mistake: Uses the wrong prefix

quiz.q: A new girl in class uses a wheelchair. What is the kind thing to do?
options: Invite her to join your group
quiz.explain: Inviting her makes her feel welcome. That is inclusion.
steps: Inclusion means no one is left out.
Invite her to join your group.
Ignoring or staring is unkind.
Answer: Invite her to join your group
quiz.mistake: Does not think about how others feel

quiz.q: Which is a respectful way to describe someone who cannot see?
options: A person who is visually impaired
A person who can do nothing
quiz.explain: We use respectful words that describe without hurting.
steps: We use kind, respectful words.
Say 'a person who is blind' or 'visually impaired'.
Answer: A person who is visually impaired
quiz.mistake: Uses words that hurt or pity people

quiz.q: In 'unhappy', which part is the prefix?
quiz.explain: The prefix 'un-' comes at the start and means 'not'.
steps: A prefix comes at the start of a word.
unhappy = un + happy.
The prefix is 'un'.
Answer: un
quiz.mistake: Does not know where a prefix goes

teach.ask: Gappu's friend Chiku cannot hear well. Gappu wants Chiku to join every game. What is inclusion, and how can Gappu help?
teach.praise: Lovely! Inclusion means everyone takes part. Gappu can be kind, invite Chiku and use signs or writing to talk. Chiku is so happy!
teach.nudge: What does inclusion mean? What can Gappu do to make sure Chiku joins in?

revise.summary: Inclusion means making sure everyone can take part. Ramps, braille signs, talking books and sign language help, and we use kind, respectful words. Prefixes like un-, dis- and im- often mean 'not'.
focus: Meaning of inclusion and ways to include everyone
remember: un + kind = unkind; dis + agree = disagree; im + possible = impossible
Say 'a person who is blind' or 'visually impaired'
traps: Leaving someone out of games is not inclusion
